claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating has an FCC matrix.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has high elastic modulus and stable wear resistance at 300 K.
Low stacking-fault energy contributes to the coating's stable room-temperature mechanical behavior.
Lattice distortion stabilizes a high dislocation density in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The critical transition temperature for the coating is estimated to lie between 400 and 600 K.
In CoCrFeMnNi, the HCP phase is energetically preferred over FCC at cryogenic temperatures, producing negative stacking-fault energy.
The stacking-fault energy of CoCrFeMnNi increases with temperature.
Increasing stacking-fault energy suppresses stacking faults and nanotwins in CoCrFeMnNi.
FeNiCrCoCu follows the same temperature-dependent stacking-fault-energy trend as CoCrFeMnNi.
At low temperature, low stacking-fault energy suppresses stacking faults in the coating.
Low stacking-fault energy favors stable planar slip and high work hardening.
A high-stacking-fault-energy regime promotes cross-slip and dislocation climb.
Suppression of stacking faults removes barriers to dislocation motion.
The loss of barriers to dislocation motion causes rapid lattice disorder and atomic diffusion.
Elevated temperature may induce amorphization or phase decomposition in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Suppression of stacking faults and loss of strain-hardening capacity cause a sharp decline in wear resistance above the critical temperature.
The elastic modulus declines sharply above the critical temperature.
Thermally stable ordered precipitates can preserve elevated-temperature strength in precipitation-strengthened HEAs.
The onset of unstable wear should coincide with a decrease in dislocation-density stability.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says thermal activation overcomes the barrier for stacking-fault formation, implying enhanced formation, whereas the mechanism says increasing temperature raises SFE and suppresses stacking-fault formation.
The initial-state and baseline fields associate low SFE with suppression of stacking faults, while the structural-mediator field says the low-SFE regime promotes planar slip and nanotwins.

The initial state attributes stability to low SFE and high dislocation density, but the mechanism does not coherently explain how rising SFE changes dislocation density; instead it jumps from stacking-fault suppression to lattice disorder and diffusion.
